content: Gentian violet is an antifungal agent approved by the FDA for treating candidal vulvovaginitis and as an antiseptic to prevent skin infections in minor cuts, scrapes, or burns. A common side effect is skin discoloration. For adults, gentian violet is indicated as a first-aid antiseptic to protect against skin infections in minor injuries. There is limited information on its off-label use, whether supported by guidelines or not. For pediatric patients, gentian violet is also indicated as a first-aid antiseptic for minor cuts, scrapes, or burns. Similar to adults, there is limited information on its off-label use, whether supported by guidelines or not. Contraindications for gentian violet are not well-documented in the drug label. It is for external use only and should not be used in the eyes, with bandages, on large areas of the body, or for more than one week unless directed by a doctor. It should not be applied to ulcerative lesions, as this may result in tattooing of the skin. If skin irritation or sensitivity develops or worsens, or if the condition persists, use should be stopped, and a doctor or pharmacist should be consulted. In cases of deep puncture wounds, animal bites, or serious burns, medical advice should be sought. Individuals known to be sensitive to any ingredients in the product should avoid its use. Adverse reactions are not well-documented in clinical trials or postmarketing data. Drug interactions are also not well-documented. There is no FDA guidance on the use of gentian violet in specific populations, including pregnant women, nursing mothers, pediatric patients, geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Similarly, there is no guidance for use in females of reproductive potential, males, or immunocompromised patients. Gentian violet is administered topically. The affected area should be cleaned, and a small amount should be applied using a cotton-tipped applicator one to three times daily. Bandaging is not recommended. Monitoring information is limited. There is no information on IV compatibility, chronic overdose, or the mechanism of action of gentian violet in the drug label. Additionally, there is limited information on its structure, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, nonclinical toxicology, and clinical studies. Gentian violet should be stored at controlled room temperature. It can stain skin and clothing. Patients should be advised to keep it out of reach of children. In case of accidental ingestion, medical help or contact with a Poison Control Center should be sought immediately. The interaction between alcohol and gentian violet has not been established. Patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while using this medication.
